```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", out.width = "100%")
options(width = 100)
```

This tutorial is for people who have never used item response theory (IRT).
It takes one domain of one cohort from the raw answers to a norm.
Then it joins two cohorts, and two domains, on one scale.

Each section starts with the question it answers.
Then comes the code.
Then comes a short note on how to read the result.

There are no formulas here.
The formulas, and the code behind each step, are in `tutorial_algorithms/`.

**The data are simulated.**
No row in this tutorial is a real child.
The demo data were drawn from summaries of the real KIT data, so they look like KIT.
But every number you see here is made up.
Do not quote these numbers as KIT results.


## 0 Before you start

**Question: what do the data look like?**

Install kits once, then load it with dplyr and purrr every session.
kits is not on CRAN; you install it from the source file.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("kits_0.23.0.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source")
```

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(kits)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
```

kits comes with two demo data sets: `kitm03` and `kitm36`.
They are the two KIT cohorts.
Cohort M03 was first seen at 3 months; cohort M36 at 36 months.
Each cohort has `r n_distinct(kitm03$responses$subj_id)` simulated children.
Each has two domains: language (`"lan"`) and motor (`"motor"`).

Each data set is a list of two tables:

* `responses`: the answers.
* `anchors`: a key that matches some KIT items to items of an international scale (used in section 10).

In `responses`, one row is one child answering one item at one visit.

```{r look}
kitm03$responses |>
  head(3)
```

The columns:

* `visit_id`: one visit, that is one child at one wave, for example `M03_c55df9b_M12`.
  kits calls this a *person-wave*.
* `subj_id`: the child, for example `c55df9b` (7 random hex characters, like a short git hash). It is the same at every visit.
  The name pairs with `item_id`: `subj_id` says who answered, `item_id` says what.
* `cohort`: `M03` or `M36`.
* `sex`: `boy` or `girl`.
* `wave_m`: the planned age of the visit, in months (the *wave*).
* `age_m`: the real age at the visit, in months. It is close to `wave_m`, but not equal.
* `item_id`: the item.
* `item_score`: the score on the item, from 0 to 3.
* `domain`: `lan` or `motor`.

Now count the children seen at each wave of each cohort.

```{r count-waves}
visits <- rbind(kitm03$responses, kitm36$responses) |>
  distinct(cohort, wave_m, visit_id)
visits |>
  count(cohort, wave_m)
```

How to read it:
M03 has waves from `r min(kitm03$responses$wave_m)` to `r max(kitm03$responses$wave_m)` months.
M36 has waves from `r min(kitm36$responses$wave_m)` to `r max(kitm36$responses$wave_m)` months.
Not every child comes to every wave, so the counts differ.

**Waves 60 and 72 of M03 are not observed.**
The real M03 cohort stops at 48 months.
In the demo, M03 at 60 and 72 months was simulated from the M36 children of that age.
These two waves show what a longer follow-up would look like.
They are not data.


## 1 One domain, one cohort: language in M03

**Question: which children answered which items?**

kits works on one domain at a time.
Keep the language answers of M03.
`kits_resp()` turns the long table into one row per person-wave and one column per item.
It also keeps the information of each child (`subj_id`, `sex`, `wave_m`, `age_m`) next to the answers.
Every later step takes this information from here, so you never align it by hand.

```{r resp}
resp <- kitm03$responses |>
  filter(domain == "lan") |>
  kits_resp()
resp
```

How to read it:
There are `r nrow(resp)` person-waves.
The second line counts them by wave.
`Checks: OK` means kits found no problem in the table.

Three words you will see from now on:

* An **item** is one task, for example "says two words together".
* A **score** is what the child got on the item. KIT items are scored 0, 1, 2 or 3. A higher score is better.
* An **item pattern** says which items one child actually answered. Most children at a wave answer the same items; kits calls that set the **standard form** of the wave. A child who skipped one item has a slightly different item pattern.

`summary()` lists every item pattern of each wave.

```{r resp-forms}
summary(resp)
```

How to read it:
Form 1 of each wave is the standard form.
`n` is the number of children who answered it, and `pct` their share of the wave.
Almost every child answered the standard form.
The other item patterns are the standard form without one item, for example `without lana05`.
`n_items` is the number of items in the item pattern.

`plot()` draws the design: which items each wave answered.

```{r resp-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(resp)
```

How to read it:
Young waves answer easy items; older waves answer harder ones.
Neighbouring waves share some items.
These shared items are what lets kits put all waves on one ruler.


## 2 The quick way: `kits()`

**Question: can I get the item thresholds and the children's scores in one step?**

Sometimes you only need the scale of one cohort, with no linking.
Then `kits()` calibrates and scores in one call.

```{r kits-fit}
fit <- kits(resp)
fit
```

How to read it:
The top part is the item table, as in section 3.
The `Abilities` line sums up the positions (θ) of the `r nrow(fit$subj)` person-waves.
Section 5 explains θ.
The `Checks:` line joins the checks of the items and of the scores.
Here it counts `r sum(fit$diagnostics$status == "warn")` warnings and `r sum(fit$diagnostics$status == "note")` notes.
Section 4 explains the item-fit note.
Section 5 explains the warnings and the other notes.

The scores are in `fit$subj`.

```{r kits-subj}
fit$subj |>
  select(visit_id, wave_m, theta, se) |>
  head(3)
```

`plot()` draws a Wright map: children on the left, item thresholds on the right.

```{r kits-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit)
```

`fit` holds two parts: `fit$item` and `fit$subj`.
They are the same as the results of `kits_item()` and `kits_subj()`.

```{r kits-parts, message = FALSE}
item_check <- kits_item(resp)
identical(coef(fit$item), coef(item_check))
identical(fit$subj$theta, kits_subj(resp, item_check)$theta)
```

Both are `TRUE`.
The rest of this tutorial does the same thing step by step.
Linking, norms and the D score need the two parts, so there you call `kits_item()` and `kits_subj()`.
Use `kits()` when you just want the scores of one cohort.


## 3 Calibration: how hard is each item?

**Question: where does each item sit on the ruler?**

*Calibration* means estimating how hard each item is, from the answers of all children at once.
kits uses the partial credit model (PCM), a common IRT model for items scored 0, 1, 2, 3.
You only give the answers.

```{r item}
item <- resp |>
  kits_item()
item
```

The *scale* is the ruler.
Its unit is the **logit**.
You do not need the definition of a logit; two facts are enough:

* Bigger means harder (for items) or more able (for children).
* The zero point is arbitrary. Each calibration sets its own zero.

So the name of the scale matters: it says which ruler the numbers are on.
We did not give a name, so kits made one from the domain and the cohort: `"`r attr(coef(item), "scale")`"`.
The message above says so.
To choose the name yourself, write `kits_item(resp, scale = "lan M03")`.
kits carries this name along to every later result.

Now look at the item table.

```{r item-coef}
coef(item) |>
  select(item_id, item_score, thr, thr_se) |>
  head(6)
```

How to read it:

* One row is one step of one item. An item scored 0 to 3 has three steps: from 0 to 1, from 1 to 2, from 2 to 3.
* `thr` (threshold) is the point on the ruler where a child has a 50% chance to reach at least this score.
* The first step (`item_score` 1) is the *milestone step*. By default kits counts a score of at least 1 as passing the item.
* `thr_se` is the uncertainty of the threshold. Smaller is more precise.

A picture of one item helps.
Here are an easy item, a middle item and a hard item.

```{r item-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(item, items = c("lana01", "lanc05", "lanb08"))
```

How to read it:
Each curve is the chance of one score.
As you move right on the ruler, low scores become less likely and high scores more likely.
The curves of the hard item sit further to the right.

The last line of the printout reads `Checks:`.
kits checks every result by itself: did the estimation converge, are there items no one passed, and so on.
`Checks: OK` would mean that all checks passed.
A `note` is for your information; a `warn` needs a look.
Here the line reports a note; `summary()` shows which check gave it.

```{r item-checks}
summary(item)
```

How to read it:
The first row says the estimation converged.
The `item fit` row is the note: `r summary(item)$diagnostics |> filter(check == "item fit") |> pull(value)` of `r nrow(item$itemfit)` items fall outside the usual range.
Section 4 looks at item fit.
All the other rows are `ok`.


::: {.optional}
### Optional: why CML needs no ability distribution

You can skip this box.
It touches lightly on how `kits_item()` estimates the items.

kits uses *conditional maximum likelihood* (CML).
CML looks at each raw score and at all the ways to reach it.
`kits_esf()` shows this for a few items; here two of them.

```{r esf}
esf <- item |>
  kits_esf(items = c("lana01", "lana02"))
esf
```

The table lists every raw score `r` the two items can give.
`gamma` ($\gamma_r$) adds up all the ways to reach that raw score.
The printout says the key point: θ cancels.

Now take the raw score in the middle.

```{r esf-prob}
esf$prob |>
  filter(r == 3)
```

How to read it:
`lana01` gets the score `x`, and `lana02` gets the rest.
So these rows are all the ways to reach this raw score, with their probabilities.
The probabilities depend only on the item parameters.
θ is not in them: every child with this raw score has the same chances.
This is why `kits_item()` assumes no distribution of ability, normal or other.
So it also works when each wave answers different items.

`plot()` draws the expected score of each item at each raw score.
Here it is for the standard form of 12 months.

```{r esf-plot, fig.height = 4}
form12 <- summary(resp)$forms |>
  filter(wave_m == 12, form == 1)
items12 <- strsplit(form12$items, ", ")[[1]]
plot(kits_esf(item, items = items12))
```

The conditional item fit of section 4 is built on these expected scores.
The formulas are in `tutorial_algorithms/`: the ESF in `01_calibration`, the item fit in `05_checks`.
:::


## 4 Do the items fit?

**Question: do the answers to each item follow the model?**

The PCM expects children to pass easy items before hard ones.
*Item fit* checks, item by item, how well the answers follow this.
`kits_item()` keeps the item fit in `item$itemfit`, one row per item.
Sort it by outfit, largest first, and show the first rows.

```{r itemfit}
item$itemfit |>
  arrange(desc(outfit)) |>
  head(5)
```

The plot shows every item, with the acceptable range shaded.

```{r itemfit-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(item, type = "fit")
```

How to read it:

* The fit is *conditional* (`attr(item$itemfit, "type")`): each answer is compared with what is expected given the child's raw score, as in the optional box above. It needs no θ.
* `infit` and `outfit` are mean squares. Near 1, the answers are as noisy as the model expects. Above 1, there are unexpected answers; below 1, the answers are more regular than expected.
* The range 0.6 to 1.4 is a rule of thumb, not a test.
* `flag` sums it up: `underfit` above the range, `overfit` below it, `ok` inside. Here: `underfit` `r sum(item$itemfit$flag == "underfit")`, `overfit` `r sum(item$itemfit$flag == "overfit")`, `ok` `r sum(item$itemfit$flag == "ok")`.
* The `Item fit:` line of the printout in section 3 counts and names the items outside this range.
* `pvalue` is the mean score as a share of the maximum; `rir` is the correlation of the item with the rest of the items.
* Children have fit too: the scores table has the columns `infit`, `outfit` and `flag` (section 5).
* `kits_itemfit(resp, item)` gives the same table. Give it other data, for example a new wave, to check the same items there.


## 5 Scoring: where is each child on the ruler?

**Question: how able is each child at each visit?**

Once the items are on the ruler, each child can be placed on the same ruler.
This is *scoring*.

```{r subj}
scores <- resp |>
  kits_subj(item)
scores
```

How to read it:

* One row is one person-wave.
* **theta** (θ) is the child's position on the ruler, in logits. A child at the same θ as a threshold has a 50% chance of reaching at least that score.
* **se** (standard error) says how precise θ is. A smaller SE means a more precise position. Roughly, the true position lies within 2 SE of θ.
* Children with the same item pattern and the same total score get the same θ.
* `flag` marks children who got 0 on every item (`zero`) or the full score (`perfect`). Their θ is less certain. `misfit` marks children whose answers do not follow the usual easy-to-hard pattern: their `infit` or `outfit` is above 2 (Linacre's rule: such answers distort the measurement). For example, a child who misses middle items but scores on the hardest one.

The method is called WLE; you do not need it now.

The last line says the scores have warnings.
`summary()` lists all checks; keep the ones that are not `ok`.

```{r subj-checks}
summary(scores)$diagnostics |>
  filter(status != "ok") |>
  select(status, check, value)
```

How to read it:
The *reliability* of a wave says how well its scores separate the children (1 is best).
It is below 0 at 3 and 6 months.
The items of these waves are too hard for many children: at 3 months,
`r sum(scores$wave_m == 3 & scores$flag == "zero")` of `r sum(scores$wave_m == 3)` children
got 0 on every item.
The `misfit` note says that `r round(100 * mean(scores$flag == "misfit"))`% of the person-waves are flagged `misfit`.

Now look at how children grow.
Average θ and SE at each wave.

```{r subj-waves}
scores |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    theta = round(mean(theta), 2),
    se = round(mean(se), 2),
    .by = wave_m
  )
```

How to read it:
Mean θ rises with age: fast in the first two years, slower later.
SE is largest at 3 months, where many children got 0 on every item.
It is larger again at 60 and 72 months, where more children got the full score.

Children and items are now on one ruler.
A *Wright map* shows both: children on one side, item thresholds on the other.

```{r wright, fig.height = 5}
plot(item, type = "wright", scores = scores)
```

How to read it:
An item next to many children is well matched to them.
Items far above all children, or far below, tell you little about them.


## 6 Raw score table

**Question: at a visit, which θ goes with each raw score?**

At a visit, the tester adds up the scores.
This sum is the *raw score*.
The raw score table gives the θ and SE for each raw score of each wave's standard form.

```{r subj-table}
raw_table <- scores |>
  kits_subj_table()
raw_table |>
  filter(wave_m == 12) |>
  select(wave_m, raw, theta, se, n)
```

How to read it:

* One row is one raw score on the standard form of one wave.
* `n` is how many children in the data had that raw score.
* The same raw score at two waves gives two different θ, because the items differ.
* Children who skipped an item are not in this table. Their θ comes from `kits_subj()`.

Without data, `kits_subj_table(item)` lists every raw score of every item pattern.
Use it to print a table for testers.


## 7 Norms: where does a child stand among children of the same age?

**Question: is this child ahead of, or behind, children of the same age?**

A **norm** describes the scores of children at each age.
Its **percentiles** are cut points.
P50 is the middle: half of the children of that age score below it.
P3 is low: only 3% score below it.
P97 is high: 97% score below it.

First, check which waves can enter a norm.
A wave where many children got the lowest score cannot show who is behind.
`kits_norm_screen()` leaves out waves with 20% or more at the lowest score.

```{r norm-screen}
screen <- scores |>
  kits_norm_screen()
screen
```

How to read it:
At 3 months, `r screen$waves$floor_pct[screen$waves$wave_m == 3]`% of the children got the lowest score.
So wave 3 is left out (`normed` is `FALSE`).

Keep the person-waves that pass the screen.

```{r norm-keep}
normed <- scores |>
  filter(screen$normed)
```

kits fits a smooth curve for each percentile, from P3 to P97, across age.
Here it fits one norm for boys and one for girls.
The age range is chosen from the data and printed.

```{r norms}
norms <- normed |>
  kits_norms(by = "sex")
print(norms, n = 3)
```

How to read it:
The message says the norms are in logits, on the ruler `"lan M03"`, not in D (section 10).
A norm in logits is fine for learning.
The second line of the printout gives the ages the norm was fitted on, and says that there is
one norm per sex.
One row is one sex at one age, every half month.
`mu`, `sigma`, `epsilon` and `delta` describe the shape of the scores at that age.
You can skip them; the percentiles are what you use.

Look at a few ages.

```{r norms-ages}
norms |>
  filter(age_m %in% c(6, 12, 24, 36, 48)) |>
  select(sex, age_m, P3, P50, P97)
```

The header still gives the ages the norm was fitted on.
`showing 10 rows` says that only the rows you kept are printed.

```{r norms-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(norms, scores = normed)
```

How to read it:
The curves rise fast early and flatten later, like the wave means in section 5.
The children should spread around the curves: about 3% below P3 and about 3% above P97.

Now compare each child with the norm.
The **z score** says how many standard deviations a child is above (+) or below (−) children of the same age and sex.
The **percentile rank** (`pct`) says what share of those children score lower.
z = 0 is the middle (50%); z = −2 is low (about 2%).

```{r norm-z}
scores_z <- scores |>
  kits_norm_z(norms)
scores_z |>
  filter(!is.na(z)) |>
  summarise(mean = round(mean(z), 2), sd = round(sd(z), 2), .by = wave_m)
```

How to read it:
At each wave, mean z should be close to 0 and SD close to 1.
If so, the norm fits the children it was made from.
Children outside the age range of the norm get `NA`.
Here that is wave 3, which the screen left out.

Now follow one child across visits.

```{r norm-z-child}
scores_z |>
  filter(subj_id == "c55df9b") |>
  select(wave_m, age_m, theta, flag, z, pct)
```

How to read it:
θ rises over the years, because the child grows.
It does not rise at every visit: each θ has an SE, so a small step down can be noise.
z stays near 0 at most visits: the child keeps its place among children of the same age.
At 60 months this child got the full score (`perfect`).
Its θ is high but uncertain, so z jumps up for one visit.
A lasting drop in z would mean the child grows more slowly than its peers.

Remember: these norms come from simulated children, and waves 60 and 72 are not observed.
They show the method, not KIT norms.


## 8 At what age do children pass each item?

**Question: at what age do half of the children pass each item?**

`kits_item_table()` fits, for each item, how the chance of passing rises with age.
It reports the age at which half of the children pass (`age50`).
It also places each item on a norm, so it needs a norm with one curve for all children.
`D` is the threshold of the item's first step (passing), here still in logits on `"lan M03"`.

```{r age-pass}
norm_all <- normed |>
  kits_norms()
item_tab <- kits_item_table(item, norm_all, data = resp)
item_tab |>
  select(item_id, D, age50) |>
  arrange(D)
```

How to read it:
`age50` is in months.
It is `NA` when, within the ages seen, the pass rate never crosses one half.
Here that happens to the items first given at 36 months: most children pass them already at their first visit.

The rows are ordered by threshold, so you can compare the two orders: by threshold and by age.
Harder items (larger `D`) are passed later (larger `age50`).
The correlation of the two orders is
`r round(cor(item_tab$D, item_tab$age50, use = "complete.obs"), 2)`.
An item out of line deserves a closer look.

`plot()` puts each item on the growth curves of the norm, at its `D` and its `age50`.

```{r age-pass-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(item_tab)
```


## 9 Two cohorts on one ruler

**Question: can M36 children be compared with M03 children?**

So far everything is on the ruler `"lan M03"`.
If you calibrate M36 by itself, you get another ruler, `"lan M36"`, with its own zero.
A θ of 1 on one ruler is not a θ of 1 on the other.
**Linking** finds the rule that moves numbers from one ruler to the other.

First, do sections 1, 3 and 5 for M36.

```{r m36}
resp36 <- kitm36$responses |>
  filter(domain == "lan") |>
  kits_resp()
item36 <- kits_item(resp36)
scores36 <- kits_subj(resp36, item36)
```

Some items were answered in both cohorts.
These *common items* have a threshold on each ruler.
kits draws a straight line through these pairs:

θ on M03 = intercept + slope × θ on M36

```{r link}
co <- kits_linking(item36, item)
co
```

How to read it:

* `scales: lan M36 -> lan M03` says the direction. Check it: the reverse is also a valid link.
* `intercept` and `slope` are the line: here intercept = `r round(co$intercept, 2)` and
  slope = `r round(co$slope, 2)`.
* Many books (Kolen & Brennan) write the line as A × θ + B, with A the slope.
  kits 0.22 and earlier called the intercept `a` and the slope `b`.
* `points` counts the common item steps used (`r co$n` here).
* `dropped` lists the steps that were far off the line and left out (`r length(co$dropped)` here).

```{r link-plot, fig.height = 4.5}
plot(co)
```

Now move the M36 scores to the M03 ruler.

```{r convert}
scores36_03 <- scores36 |>
  kits_convert(co)
print(scores36_03, n = 3)
```

The column is still called `theta`.
Only the ruler changed; the printout and `attr(, "scale")` say which.

The two cohorts overlap from 36 to 72 months.
If the link works, children of the same age should have about the same mean in both cohorts.
Stack the two tables with `rbind()`.

```{r overlap}
both <- rbind(scores, scores36_03)
both |>
  filter(wave_m %in% c(36, 48, 60, 72)) |>
  summarise(theta = round(mean(theta), 2), .by = c(wave_m, cohort)) |>
  arrange(wave_m)
```

How to read it:
At 36 and 48 months the two means are close.
Both cohorts were observed at these ages, so 36 and 48 are the fair check.
At 60 and 72, M03 was simulated from M36, so these rows do not test the link.

kits refuses to stack tables on different rulers.
If you forget `kits_convert()`, `rbind()` stops with an error.
This is on purpose.

```{r rbind-error, error = TRUE}
rbind(scores, scores36)
```

`kits_vertical()` sums up each cohort at each wave.
Its plot shows the two cohorts on one ruler.

```{r vertical, fig.height = 4.5}
plot(kits_vertical(both), type = "median")
```

How to read it:
Each point is the median θ of one cohort at one wave; the bar runs from P25 to P75.
Where the cohorts overlap, their points should nearly meet.
The line goes on to 96 months with M36 alone.


## 10 Two domains, and the D score

**Question: how do we report language and motor on one international scale?**

So far you did one domain step by step.
Now do language and motor together.
`purrr::map()` runs the same steps for each domain; `list_rbind()` stacks the results.

```{r domains-items}
resps <- c("lan", "motor") |>
  set_names() |>
  map(\(d) kits_resp(filter(kitm03$responses, domain == d)))
items <- resps |>
  map(kits_item)
```

The **D score** is the developmental score of the GSED (Global Scales for Early Development), from the WHO.
Its unit is D.
Putting KIT on D lets KIT be compared with other countries.

Some KIT items are the same as GSED items.
These are the **anchor items**.
Each has a known GSED difficulty, `tau`, in D.
The key is already in the data: `kitm03$anchors`.

```{r anchors}
used <- kitm03$responses |>
  distinct(item_id, domain)
n_anchors <- kitm03$anchors |>
  semi_join(used, by = c("item_id", "domain")) |>
  count(domain)
n_anchors
```

How to read it:
In M03, motor has `r n_anchors$n[n_anchors$domain == "motor"]` anchors
and language only `r n_anchors$n[n_anchors$domain == "lan"]`.
A link needs at least 3 anchors.
So language cannot be linked to D on its own:

```{r d-link-lan, error = TRUE}
kits_linking(items$lan, kitm03$anchors)
```

This is one reason to link the domains together, with one shared line.
Give `kits_linking()` the named list of both calibrations.

```{r d-link}
d_link <- kits_linking(items, kitm03$anchors)
d_link
```

How to read it:

* D = intercept + slope × θ, with θ on each domain's M03 ruler.
  Here intercept = `r round(d_link$intercept, 1)` and slope = `r round(d_link$slope, 1)`.
* `kept points by domain` shows that most anchors come from motor.
* The domain check fits each domain its own intercept, as a check.
* The intercepts (`r round(d_link$domains$intercept, 1)`) are close to the shared `intercept`, so one line for both domains is reasonable.

Now score both domains and convert to D.

```{r d-scores}
d_scores <- map2(resps, items, kits_subj) |>
  map(\(s) kits_convert(s, d_link)) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "domain")
print(d_scores, n = 3)
```

The scale is now `D` for both domains.
Put the mean D of each domain at each wave in one table.

```{r d-table}
d_scores |>
  summarise(D = round(mean(theta), 1), .by = c(wave_m, domain)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = domain, values_from = D)
```

How to read it:
Both domains are now in D, so their means can sit in one table.
D rises with age in both domains.

M36 reaches D through two links: first `co` (M36 to M03), then `d_link` (M03 to D).
Give both links to `kits_convert()`, in the order they apply.

```{r d-m36}
scores36_d <- scores36 |>
  kits_convert(co, d_link)
scores36_d |>
  summarise(D = round(mean(theta), 1), .by = wave_m) |>
  arrange(wave_m)
```

How to read it:
At 36 and 48 months, M36 language should be close to M03 language in the table above.
After 72 months, only M36 goes on.


## 11 Next steps

* **Real KIT data**: `tutorial_kit/`. Same steps, with the real response files, norm screening and more checks.
* **Formulas and code**: `tutorial_algorithms/`, in six parts (calibration, scoring, linking, norms, checks, scale). Each step written as a formula, as code, and checked by hand. `kits_algorithm(x)` says how any result `x` was made: its steps, formulas, functions and references.
* **Other packages**: `tutorial_compare/` compares kits with TAM. kitsPreview runs the same steps with dexter or immer.
* **More in kits**: `vignette("kits-flow", package = "kits")` and `vignette("kits-advanced", package = "kits")` cover item fit, DIF, linking error, new waves and the checks (`kits_check()`, `kits_info()`).


## Words used in this tutorial

| Word | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| Item | One task the child is asked to do. |
| Score | What the child got on one item: 0, 1, 2, ... |
| Raw score | The sum of the item scores of one visit. |
| Item pattern | Which items one child answered at one visit. |
| Standard form | The item pattern most children of a wave answered. |
| Person-wave, visit | One child at one wave (`visit_id`). |
| Calibration | Estimating how hard each item is, from all answers at once. |
| Scale, ruler | The line on which items and children are placed. It has a name, like `"lan M03"`. |
| Logit | The unit of a calibrated scale. Its zero is arbitrary. |
| Threshold (`thr`) | The point on the ruler where a child has a 50% chance to reach at least this score. |
| Item fit (infit, outfit) | How well the answers to an item follow the model. Near 1 is good. |
| θ (theta) | A child's position on the ruler. |
| SE | How precise a θ or a threshold is. Smaller is more precise. |
| Reliability | How well the scores of a wave separate the children. 1 is best. |
| Age at 50% passing (`p50`) | The age at which half of the children pass an item. |
| Norm | The spread of scores of children at each age. |
| Percentile (P3 ... P97) | The score below which 3%, ..., 97% of same-age children fall. |
| z score | How many SDs a child is above or below same-age children. |
| Percentile rank (`pct`) | The share of same-age children who score lower. |
| Common items | Items answered in both cohorts. |
| Linking | Finding the straight line that moves numbers from one ruler to another. |
| Anchor items | KIT items that are also GSED items, with a known difficulty in D. |
| D score | The GSED developmental scale. Its unit is D. |
